title: Canada Post Text Scam
metaTitle: Canada Post Text Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Learn common red flags of Canada Post text scams, example message patterns, and what to do if you clicked a suspicious link or paid a fake fee.
summary: This scam sends a fake Canada Post delivery notice asking you to click a link or pay a small redelivery fee, then collects your card and personal details on a fake page.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: An unexpected delivery text asking you to pay a fee or confirm details through a link.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not click the link. Check any delivery using the official Canada Post website or app.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'CANADA POST: Your parcel could not be delivered due to an unpaid fee of $1.45. Update your details here: [suspicious link]'
redFlags: An unexpected delivery message when you may not be expecting a parcel
A small redelivery or 'unpaid fee' request
A link that does not lead to the official canadapost.ca domain
Urgent wording warning the parcel will be returned
A request for personal or card information to reschedule delivery
whatToDo: Do not click the link or enter any details
Check your tracking number directly on the official Canada Post website or app
Forward the text to your mobile provider's spam reporting service if available
Delete the message and block the sender
ifYouClicked: Do not enter any more information on the page
If you entered card details, contact your bank to flag or freeze the card
Change the password for any account where you reused that login
Watch your statements for unexpected charges
whatNotToDo: Do not reply to the message
Do not share verification codes
Do not download any app the link suggests

faqs.question: Does Canada Post charge fees by text message?
faqs.answer: Genuine redelivery is normally arranged for free, and any real charge can be confirmed through the official Canada Post website. A small fee demanded through a text link is a common scam pattern.

faqs.question: I am expecting a parcel, so is the text real?
faqs.answer: Scammers count on this. Even if you are expecting something, check the tracking number on the official site rather than using the link in the text.

faqs.question: What if I already paid the fee?
faqs.answer: Contact your bank right away to report the transaction and protect your card. The sooner you act, the more likely the charge can be stopped or disputed.

faqs.question: How can I report a Canada Post text scam?
faqs.answer: You can report it to your mobile provider, to Canada Post through its official fraud page, and to your national anti-fraud centre.

title: Fake Delivery Text Scam
metaTitle: Fake Delivery Text Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Spot fake delivery text scams that impersonate couriers like UPS, FedEx, and DHL. See example patterns, red flags, and safe steps to take.
summary: This scam impersonates a courier with a missed-delivery text and a link to a fake page that asks for a fee or your personal and card details.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A missed-delivery text with a link from a number or address that is not the courier's official channel.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not click. Track the parcel through the courier's official website or app.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'Your package is held at our depot. Please confirm your delivery preferences: [suspicious link]'
redFlags: A delivery alert from a courier you did not order from
A link that does not match the courier's official website
A request to pay a fee or confirm card details to release the parcel
Generic wording that never names the retailer or item
Pressure to act before the parcel is 'returned to sender'
whatToDo: Do not click the link or pay any fee
Find the retailer's order confirmation and use its official tracking
Verify with the courier through its official website or app
Report and delete the message
ifYouClicked: Stop and do not submit any details on the page
Contact your bank if you entered card information
Change any password you may have entered
Monitor your accounts for unusual activity
whatNotToDo: Do not reply to confirm your number is active
Do not share one-time codes
Do not install apps the message asks you to download

faqs.question: How do scammers know I am expecting a delivery?
faqs.answer: In most cases they do not. These texts are sent in bulk, and with so many people shopping online, some recipients happen to be waiting for a parcel.

faqs.question: Are all courier texts fake?
faqs.answer: No. Couriers do send genuine updates. The warning signs are unexpected fees, mismatched links, and requests for personal or card details.

faqs.question: How can I tell the real courier site from a fake one?
faqs.answer: Type the courier's address yourself or use its official app instead of tapping the link. Check the web address carefully for misspellings and extra words.

faqs.question: What should I do if I shared my address only?
faqs.answer: An address alone is low risk, but stay alert for follow-up scam messages and never share codes, passwords, or card details in response.

title: PayPal Payment Pending Scam
metaTitle: PayPal Payment Pending Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Understand the PayPal payment pending scam, how fake 'release the funds' emails work, and what to do to protect your money and account.
summary: This scam shows a fake 'payment on hold' message claiming funds will be released once you ship an item or confirm details, but no real payment exists.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A 'pending' PayPal payment that asks you to ship goods or confirm details before money actually arrives.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Log in to PayPal directly to check your real balance. Do not act on the email alone.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'The buyer's payment of $480.00 is pending and will be released to your account once you provide the shipment tracking number. Reply to confirm.'
redFlags: A 'pending' or 'on hold' payment you cannot see in your real PayPal balance
A request to ship an item before the money has actually cleared
Emails from an address that is not an official PayPal domain
Pressure to act quickly to 'release' the funds
A request to send a shipping or release fee first
whatToDo: Open PayPal directly in your browser or app and check your real balance
Treat money as received only when it appears in your actual account
Do not ship anything based on an email alone
Report suspicious emails to PayPal and delete them
ifYouClicked: Do not enter your login on any linked page
If you logged in, change your PayPal password immediately
Turn on two-factor authentication for your account
Review recent activity and contact PayPal if anything looks wrong
whatNotToDo: Do not ship goods before funds clear in your real account
Do not send a 'release' or shipping fee
Do not share your password or verification codes

faqs.question: Does PayPal hold funds until I add tracking?
faqs.answer: PayPal may place genuine holds on some payments, but you will always see this inside your real account. A request that exists only in an email and asks you to ship first is a scam pattern.

faqs.question: Why does the email look so real?
faqs.answer: Scammers copy logos, wording, and layout. The reliable check is to ignore the email and log in to PayPal directly to confirm your actual balance and any holds.

faqs.question: A buyer says they paid but I see nothing. What now?
faqs.answer: Do not ship. If the money is not in your real PayPal balance, treat it as unpaid, and be cautious if the buyer pressures you to send the item.

faqs.question: How do I report a fake PayPal email?
faqs.answer: Forward it to PayPal's official phishing reporting address and then delete it. Do not click any links inside it.

title: Facebook Marketplace Buyer Email Scam
metaTitle: Facebook Marketplace Buyer Email Scam: Red Flags
metaDescription: Learn how the Facebook Marketplace buyer email scam works, with example fake-payment patterns and steps to sell safely without losing money.
summary: A fake buyer claims to have paid through an email service and asks you to confirm a fee or send the 'difference' before any real money arrives.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: An emailed 'payment confirmation' that asks you to send a fee or refund before money is in your account.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Ignore the email. Only treat a sale as paid when funds clear in your own bank or platform account.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'PayPal has received the buyer's payment of $650. To release it, the seller must first send a $50 shipping insurance fee and reply with the receipt.'
redFlags: A buyer who insists on paying by email service instead of the platform
An emailed 'confirmation' you cannot see in your real account
A request to pay a shipping, insurance, or release fee first
Overpayment with a request to refund the difference
Pressure to ship quickly before the money clears
whatToDo: Keep the conversation and payment inside the platform where possible
Confirm money has actually cleared in your own account before shipping
Decline requests to pay any upfront fee to 'release' funds
Report the buyer and block them
ifYouClicked: Do not log in on any page linked from the email
Change your password if you entered login details
Contact your bank if you sent any money or shared card details
Report the scam to the platform
whatNotToDo: Do not send any fee to release a payment
Do not refund an 'overpayment' you never actually received
Do not move the deal to email or text to bypass platform protections

faqs.question: Why does the buyer want to use email instead of the app?
faqs.answer: Moving off-platform removes reporting tools and protections and lets the scammer send fake 'confirmation' emails that look official but are not tied to any real payment.

faqs.question: The email looks like it is from PayPal. Is it genuine?
faqs.answer: Scammers forge these emails. Verify by logging in to your real account. If the money is not there, no payment has been made.

faqs.question: Is overpayment ever legitimate?
faqs.answer: Genuine buyers rarely overpay and then ask for a refund of the difference. This is a classic scam designed to get you to send real money against a fake payment.

faqs.question: How can I sell more safely on Marketplace?
faqs.answer: Prefer local pickup with cash in a safe public place, keep payments on-platform, and never send a fee to release funds.

title: Fake Job Offer Scam
metaTitle: Fake Job Offer Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Recognise fake job offer scams that hire with no real interview and ask for fees or bank details. See example patterns and safety steps.
summary: This scam offers a job with little or no interview, then asks for upfront fees, personal documents, or bank details to 'set you up.'

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A job offer with no real interview that asks for money or bank details upfront.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Pause. Verify the company independently and never pay to get a job.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'Congratulations! You have been selected for a remote position paying $35/hour. To begin onboarding, please pay a $90 refundable equipment deposit and send a photo of your ID.'
redFlags: A job offer arriving with no interview or only a brief chat-app exchange
Pay that is high for very simple work
A request for an upfront fee for equipment, training, or a background check
A request for bank details or ID before any real hiring process
A recruiter who only communicates through a messaging app
whatToDo: Search for the company and contact it through its official website
Refuse to pay any fee to be hired
Be cautious sharing ID or bank details until the employer is verified
Report suspicious recruiters to the platform where they contacted you
ifYouClicked: Stop sharing any further documents or details
Contact your bank if you sent money or shared account details
Change passwords if you entered them on a fake onboarding page
Watch your accounts and credit for unexpected activity
whatNotToDo: Do not pay for a job, training, or equipment
Do not send copies of your ID to unverified recruiters
Do not agree to receive and forward money for an 'employer'

faqs.question: Should a real employer ever ask me to pay them?
faqs.answer: No. Legitimate employers do not require upfront payment for equipment, training, or onboarding as a condition of being hired.

faqs.question: Is a refundable deposit safe?
faqs.answer: Calling a fee 'refundable' is a common trick. Once you pay, the money and the recruiter usually disappear.

faqs.question: Why would a job want my bank details so early?
faqs.answer: Genuine payroll details are collected after you are formally hired through proper channels. Early requests can be used for fraud or to set up money-mule activity.

faqs.question: How can I verify a job offer?
faqs.answer: Look up the company independently, check that the recruiter's email uses the company domain, and be wary of roles handled entirely through chat apps.

title: Instagram Verification Scam
metaTitle: Instagram Verification Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Learn how the Instagram verification scam uses fake badge offers and warnings to steal logins. See example patterns and how to stay safe.
summary: This scam offers a blue verification badge or warns your account is at risk, then links to a fake login page that steals your password.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A DM or email offering verification or warning of account loss through an outside link.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not log in through the link. Manage verification only inside the official app.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'Your account is eligible for the verified badge. Complete verification within 24 hours or your eligibility expires: [suspicious link]'
redFlags: A message promising a verification badge through an outside link
A warning that your account will be deleted unless you 'verify' now
A login page on a web address that is not the official platform
A request for your password, email, or two-factor code
Urgent deadlines designed to make you act fast
whatToDo: Ignore the link and open the app directly
Manage verification only through official in-app settings
Turn on two-factor authentication
Report the message as spam or phishing
ifYouClicked: Change your password immediately from the official app
Log out other sessions and review login activity
Turn on two-factor authentication if it is not already on
Warn contacts if your account may have sent messages
whatNotToDo: Do not enter your password on a linked page
Do not share two-factor codes with anyone
Do not authorise unknown apps to access your account

faqs.question: Does Instagram offer verification by DM?
faqs.answer: Verification is handled inside the official app, not through unsolicited DMs with outside links. Such messages are almost always phishing.

faqs.question: Why is there a countdown or deadline?
faqs.answer: Urgency is a manipulation tactic. It pressures you to act before you have time to question whether the offer is real.

faqs.question: I entered my password. What now?
faqs.answer: Change it immediately, turn on two-factor authentication, and review your active sessions and login activity from the official app.

faqs.question: How can I protect my account?
faqs.answer: Use a strong unique password, enable two-factor authentication, and never log in through links sent in DMs or emails.

title: Fake Bank Alert Text Scam
metaTitle: Fake Bank Alert Text Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Recognise fake bank alert text scams that warn of suspicious activity to steal logins and codes. See example patterns and how to verify safely.
summary: This scam sends a text claiming suspicious activity on your account, then steers you to a fake login page or a 'fraud agent' who pressures you to move money.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A text about fraud on your account that links to a login page or asks for a code.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not use the link. Call your bank using the number on your card.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'ALERT: A payment of $720 to NEW PAYEE was authorised. If this was not you, verify now: [suspicious link]'
redFlags: A text warning of fraud and urging you to act immediately
A link to a login page that is not your bank's official site or app
A follow-up call asking you to read out a one-time code
Pressure to move money to a 'safe' or 'new' account
A request for your full card number, PIN, or online banking password
whatToDo: Do not click the link or call numbers from the text
Call your bank using the number on the back of your card or in its official app
Check your account through the official app, not the message
Report the text to your bank and delete it
ifYouClicked: Contact your bank immediately using its official number
Change your online banking password
Ask the bank to review recent activity and secure your account
Watch for further suspicious calls pretending to 'help'
whatNotToDo: Do not share one-time passcodes or your PIN
Do not move money because someone told you to
Do not log in through links in the text

faqs.question: Will my bank ask me to move money to keep it safe?
faqs.answer: No. A genuine bank will never tell you to move your money to another account to protect it. This instruction is a clear sign of a scam.

faqs.question: Should I ever read out a one-time code?
faqs.answer: Never share one-time codes with anyone, including someone claiming to be from your bank. These codes authorise access and payments.

faqs.question: The text shows my bank's name. Is it genuine?
faqs.answer: Scammers can spoof sender names so a fake text appears in the same thread as real ones. Always verify through the official app or phone number instead.

faqs.question: How do I report a fake bank text?
faqs.answer: Report it to your bank through its official fraud line and to your national anti-fraud or spam-text service, then delete it.

title: Fake Online Store Scam
metaTitle: Fake Online Store Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Spot fake online store scams that advertise cheap deals and take your money. See example patterns, red flags, and how to check a website.
summary: This scam sets up a convincing but fake store with very low prices, takes payment, and delivers nothing, a counterfeit, or a cheap substitute.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: Unrealistically low prices on a new store with only risky payment options.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Research the store before paying, and prefer payment methods with buyer protection.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'CLOSING DOWN SALE - 80% off everything today only! Limited stock, order now before it's gone: [unfamiliar store link]'
redFlags: Prices far below normal for popular brands
A brand-new website with no genuine reviews or address
Only wire transfer, gift card, or cryptocurrency accepted
Countdown timers and 'almost sold out' pressure
Poor grammar, copied images, or missing contact details
whatToDo: Search the store name with words like 'scam' or 'review'
Check how long the website has existed and look for real contact details
Prefer payment methods that offer buyer protection
Walk away if anything feels rushed or unclear
ifYouClicked: Stop before entering card details if anything seems off
Contact your bank or card provider to dispute a payment if you already paid
Change your password if you created an account with a reused password
Keep records of the order and any messages
whatNotToDo: Do not pay by wire transfer, gift card, or crypto for online shopping
Do not ignore the lack of reviews or contact details
Do not enter card details on a site you cannot verify

faqs.question: How can I check if an online store is legitimate?
faqs.answer: Look for a real contact address, search the store name with 'review' or 'scam', and check how long the domain has existed. Be wary if only risky payment methods are offered.

faqs.question: Why are the prices so low?
faqs.answer: Very low prices are bait. The goal is to make you act quickly before you research the store or notice missing details.

faqs.question: I paid and nothing arrived. What can I do?
faqs.answer: Contact your bank or card provider to dispute the charge, keep all records, and report the store to consumer protection authorities.

faqs.question: Are social media ads for stores safe?
faqs.answer: Ads are not vetted guarantees of legitimacy. Treat unfamiliar stores from ads with the same caution and research them before buying.

title: Rental Deposit Scam
metaTitle: Rental Deposit Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Avoid rental deposit scams that demand money before a viewing. See example patterns, red flags, and how to verify a listing safely.
summary: This scam advertises a desirable rental at a low price and demands a deposit before any viewing, then disappears once you pay.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A request for a deposit or holding fee before you have viewed the property.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not pay anything before viewing and verifying the landlord.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'I'm currently abroad so I can't show the apartment, but I can mail the keys once you send the first month's rent and deposit by e-transfer to hold it.'
redFlags: A landlord who cannot show the property in person or by live video
A deposit or holding fee demanded before any viewing
Rent that is unusually cheap for the area
Pressure to pay fast because of 'other interested tenants'
Payment requested by wire transfer, e-transfer, or gift card
whatToDo: Insist on viewing the property before paying anything
Verify the landlord owns or manages the property
Search the listing photos to check they are not copied
Use traceable payment and get a signed agreement after viewing
ifYouClicked: Stop any further payments immediately
Contact your bank or e-transfer provider to try to recall the funds
Keep all messages, listings, and receipts as evidence
Report the listing to the platform and local authorities
whatNotToDo: Do not pay a deposit before viewing
Do not send money by gift card or wire transfer to hold a rental
Do not share ID or bank details with an unverified landlord

faqs.question: Should I ever pay before seeing a rental?
faqs.answer: Avoid paying any deposit or fee before you have viewed the property and confirmed the landlord's right to rent it. Legitimate landlords expect you to view first.

faqs.question: The landlord says they are abroad. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: An absent landlord who cannot arrange any viewing but wants money upfront is a common scam setup. Be very cautious.

faqs.question: How can I tell if a listing is stolen?
faqs.answer: Search the listing photos and description online. If they appear elsewhere under different names or prices, the listing may be fake.

faqs.question: What payment methods are safest for rentals?
faqs.answer: Avoid wire transfers, e-transfers, and gift cards, which are hard to reverse. Use traceable methods and only after viewing and signing an agreement.

title: Wrong Number Text Scam
metaTitle: Wrong Number Text Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Understand the wrong number text scam, how friendly 'mistaken' texts lead to investment fraud, and what to do if you replied.
summary: This scam starts with a friendly 'wrong number' text, builds a casual conversation over time, and eventually steers you toward a fake investment.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A stranger's 'wrong number' text that keeps chatting and later mentions investments.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not reply. Block and delete the message.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'Hi Jessica, are we still on for lunch tomorrow?' Then, after you reply that they have the wrong number: 'Oh sorry! You seem nice though, where are you from?'
redFlags: An unsolicited text from an unknown number that seems like a mistake
A friendly stranger who keeps the conversation going after the 'mistake'
Questions designed to build rapport over days or weeks
An eventual mention of crypto or an investment opportunity
Photos and stories that seem too polished or rehearsed
whatToDo: Do not reply, even to say they have the wrong number
Block the number and delete the conversation
Be especially wary if any investment is mentioned
Report the number to your provider's spam service
ifYouClicked: Stop communicating if you have started a conversation
Do not send any money or download any trading app they suggest
If you invested, contact your bank and stop further payments
Keep records and report to your anti-fraud centre
whatNotToDo: Do not continue chatting out of politeness
Do not click links or install apps they recommend
Do not send money or crypto to someone you met this way

faqs.question: Is replying to a wrong number text dangerous?
faqs.answer: Replying confirms your number is active and signals you may engage. With scam texts it is safer not to reply and to block the number.

faqs.question: What is the goal of a wrong number text?
faqs.answer: Many lead to long-term confidence scams that gradually steer you toward fake crypto or investment platforms, sometimes called 'pig butchering' scams.

faqs.question: They seem genuine and friendly. Could it be real?
faqs.answer: Scammers invest weeks building trust. A friendly tone is part of the method, so be cautious with any stranger who reached you by accident and keeps chatting.

faqs.question: What if I already sent money?
faqs.answer: Stop all further payments, contact your bank immediately, and report it. Be wary of anyone who promises to recover your funds for a fee.

title: Fake Toll Road Text Scam
metaTitle: Fake Toll Road Text Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Spot fake toll road text scams demanding payment for unpaid tolls. See example patterns, red flags, and how to check real toll charges.
summary: This scam texts you about a small unpaid toll and threatens late fees, linking to a fake page that collects your card and personal details.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A text about an unpaid toll with a link and threat of late fees.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not click. Check any toll account through the official toll operator's website.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'You have an outstanding toll charge of $4.20. To avoid a late fee of $50, pay now: [suspicious link]'
redFlags: A toll charge text for a road or account you do not recognise
A small amount due with a large 'late fee' threat
A link that is not the official toll operator's website
A request for card details and personal information
Urgent deadlines to pay within hours
whatToDo: Do not click the link or enter card details
Look up the official toll operator and check your account directly
Report the text to your mobile provider's spam service
Delete the message and block the sender
ifYouClicked: Do not submit any details on the page
Contact your bank if you entered card information
Change passwords for any reused logins
Monitor your statements for unexpected charges
whatNotToDo: Do not pay through the link in the text
Do not share card or personal details
Do not reply to the message

faqs.question: How do I know if I really owe a toll?
faqs.answer: Look up the official toll operator for your area and log in to your account there. Do not rely on a link in a text message.

faqs.question: Why is the toll amount so small?
faqs.answer: A small, believable amount lowers your guard, while the threat of a large late fee pressures you to pay quickly through the fake page.

faqs.question: I do not even use toll roads. Why did I get this?
faqs.answer: These texts are sent in bulk to many numbers at random, so receiving one does not mean you owe anything.

faqs.question: What if I entered my card details?
faqs.answer: Contact your bank immediately to flag the card and watch for unauthorised charges.

title: Fake E-Transfer Scam
metaTitle: Fake E-Transfer Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Recognise fake e-transfer scams with phishing 'deposit' emails that steal banking logins. See example patterns and how to deposit safely.
summary: This scam sends a fake e-transfer notification linking to a phishing page that imitates your bank's login to steal your online banking details.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: An e-transfer 'deposit' email that asks you to log in through its link.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not use the email link. Deposit through your bank's official app or website.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'INTERAC e-Transfer: You have received $250.00. Click here to deposit your funds: [suspicious link]'
redFlags: An e-transfer from someone you do not know or were not expecting
A 'deposit' link that opens a bank login page rather than your app
A web address that is not your bank's official site
A request for your card number, password, or security questions
Pressure to deposit quickly before it 'expires'
whatToDo: Open your bank's official app or website to receive transfers
Use auto-deposit so you never click an email link
Verify any unexpected transfer with the supposed sender
Report the phishing email to your bank and delete it
ifYouClicked: Do not enter your banking details on the linked page
If you logged in, change your online banking password immediately
Call your bank to secure your account
Review recent activity for anything unexpected
whatNotToDo: Do not enter banking logins on emailed links
Do not share security question answers
Do not accept transfers from unknown senders

faqs.question: How can I receive e-transfers safely?
faqs.answer: Set up auto-deposit with your bank so funds arrive automatically without any link, and access transfers only through your official banking app or website.

faqs.question: The email looks like my bank. Is it real?
faqs.answer: Scammers copy bank branding closely. The safe approach is to ignore the link and check directly in your official banking app.

faqs.question: Why would a stranger send me money?
faqs.answer: They are not really sending money. The 'deposit' link leads to a fake login page designed to capture your banking credentials.

faqs.question: I entered my banking login. What now?
faqs.answer: Change your password immediately, call your bank to secure the account, and watch for unauthorised transactions.

title: WhatsApp Job Scam
metaTitle: WhatsApp Job Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Recognise WhatsApp job scams offering easy paid tasks that lead to deposits and lost money. See example patterns and safety steps.
summary: This scam contacts you on WhatsApp with an easy paid-task job, shows small early 'earnings,' then asks you to deposit money to unlock bigger payouts.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: An unsolicited WhatsApp job offering easy money that later asks you to deposit funds.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not engage or deposit anything. Block and report the contact.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'Hi, I'm a recruiter from a marketing agency. Earn $200-$500 daily completing simple app tasks from home. Interested? No experience needed.'
redFlags: An unsolicited job message on WhatsApp or Telegram
Very high pay for simple, repetitive tasks
Small early payouts to build trust
A request to deposit your own money to 'unlock' tasks or withdrawals
Pressure to recruit others or act quickly
whatToDo: Do not deposit any money or complete 'tasks'
Block and report the contact on the messaging app
Verify any company independently through its official website
Warn friends who may receive similar messages
ifYouClicked: Stop depositing immediately, even to recover earlier deposits
Contact your bank or payment provider to stop further payments
Keep screenshots of the chat and any platform used
Report the scam to your anti-fraud centre
whatNotToDo: Do not deposit money to 'unlock' withdrawals
Do not send more to recover what you already paid
Do not share bank or crypto wallet details

faqs.question: Why did the first small payout work?
faqs.answer: Early payouts are bait to build trust so you deposit larger amounts. Once you do, withdrawals stop and more 'fees' are demanded.

faqs.question: Is a real job ever found through a cold WhatsApp message?
faqs.answer: Genuine recruiters rarely cold-message offers of huge daily pay for trivial tasks. Treat such messages as scams.

faqs.question: They asked me to recruit friends. Why?
faqs.answer: Recruitment spreads the scam and can make you appear responsible for others' losses. Do not invite anyone.

faqs.question: Can I get my deposits back?
faqs.answer: Recovery is difficult. Stop paying immediately, report it, and be wary of anyone promising to recover funds for a fee, which is often a second scam.

title: Fake Invoice Email Scam
metaTitle: Fake Invoice Email Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Recognise fake invoice email scams that bill you for purchases you never made. See example patterns, red flags, and safe steps to take.
summary: This scam emails an invoice or receipt for something you did not buy, hoping you call a fake 'support' number or click a link to dispute it.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: An invoice or receipt for a purchase you never made, with a number to call to cancel.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not call the number or click links. Check the real account directly.

faqs.question: Does UPS charge delivery fees by text?
faqs.answer: Most genuine charges are arranged when you place an order or through the official UPS site, not demanded by a surprise text. A small fee requested through a text link is a common scam pattern.

faqs.question: The text has a tracking number, so is it genuine?
faqs.answer: Scammers often add a random or fake tracking number to look convincing. Always check the number on the official UPS site rather than trusting the link.

faqs.question: What if I already entered my card details?
faqs.answer: Contact your bank immediately to report it and protect your card. The sooner you act, the better the chance the charge can be blocked or disputed.

faqs.question: How do I report a UPS text scam?
faqs.answer: You can report it to UPS through its official fraud reporting page, to your mobile provider, and to your national anti-fraud centre.

quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not tap the link. Check voicemail the way you normally do, through your phone's dialler or your provider's official app.

Sender details, spelling, or a link that does not match your phone provider
whatToDo: Do not tap the link or sign in through it
Check your voicemail directly through your phone or your provider's official app
Compare the sender against your provider's known contact details

ifYouClicked: Close the page and do not enter your login or account details

whatNotToDo: Do not enter your email or account password on the linked page

faqs.question: Do real voicemail alerts contain links to click?
faqs.answer: Genuine voicemail usually appears in your phone's dialler or your provider's app, not as a text or email with a sign-in link. A link to 'listen' is a common phishing pattern.

faqs.question: It mentions a real missed call, so is it genuine?
faqs.answer: A vague missed-call or voicemail claim can apply to almost anyone. Check your actual voicemail through your phone rather than trusting the message.

faqs.question: What is the link usually trying to do?
faqs.answer: It often leads to a fake login page that captures your email or account password, or it tries to get you to install an app. Neither is needed to hear a real voicemail.

faqs.question: How do I report a fake voicemail text?
faqs.answer: You can forward it to your mobile provider's spam reporting service, report phishing emails to your email provider, and notify your national anti-fraud centre.

title: Two-Factor Code Text Scam
metaTitle: Two-Factor Code Text Scam: Red Flags & Tips
metaDescription: Learn how two-factor code text scams work, see an example pattern, and find out why you should never share a one-time verification code with anyone.
summary: In this scam a fraudster triggers a genuine two-factor or one-time code to your phone, then poses as support staff or a contact to pressure you into reading it back so they can take over your account.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: Someone asking you to share a verification or one-time code that just arrived, no matter the reason they give.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not share the code. A genuine company or contact will never need you to read a code back to them.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'This is account security. We detected a login attempt and sent you a 6-digit code. Please read it back to us so we can secure your account.'
redFlags: A verification code arrives when you did not just try to log in yourself
Someone contacts you and asks you to read that code back to them
Pressure or urgency, such as a warning that your account is being hacked right now
A 'contact' messaging from an unusual number or account asking for a code to 'verify' something
The caller or message claims to be support but reached out to you first
whatToDo: Do not share the code with anyone, even if they sound official or familiar
Treat an unexpected code as a sign someone may have your password and change it
Turn on app-based or hardware two-factor authentication where possible
Contact the company directly using a number or app you trust, not one the caller gave
ifYouClicked: If you shared a code, change that account's password immediately from a trusted device
Sign out of all active sessions in the account's security settings
Check and remove any unfamiliar recovery emails, phone numbers, or linked devices
Warn anyone whose account was used to message you, as it may be compromised
whatNotToDo: Do not read a code aloud or type it into a chat for anyone
Do not trust caller ID or a familiar name, as both can be faked
Do not assume an unexpected code is harmless and ignore it

faqs.question: Will a real company ever ask for my verification code?
faqs.answer: Legitimate companies do not phone or message you to ask for a one-time code. The code is meant for you alone, so any request to share it is a strong warning sign.

faqs.question: Why did I get a code I did not request?
faqs.answer: It often means someone has your password and is trying to log in. They then need your code to finish, which is why they may contact you pretending to be support.

faqs.question: A friend asked me for a code they 'accidentally' sent me, is that safe?
faqs.answer: Be cautious. Their account may be hacked and used to harvest codes. Confirm through another channel before sharing anything, and usually you should not share it at all.

faqs.question: What should I do after refusing to share a code?
faqs.answer: Change the password for the account the code was for, enable stronger two-factor protection, and review the account's recent activity and security settings.

A link that does not lead to the official amazon domain you normally use
An amount designed to alarm you into reacting quickly
A request for your Amazon login, card, or one-time code to stop the charge
whatToDo: Do not call the number or tap the link in the message
Sign in to Amazon through the official app or website and check your membership and orders
Report the text to Amazon through its official reporting channel and to your mobile provider
Delete the message and block the sender
ifYouClicked: Do not enter login or card details on the linked page
If you signed in, change your Amazon password from a trusted device and enable two-factor authentication
If you gave card details, contact your bank to flag or freeze the card
Review your Amazon orders and payment methods for changes you did not make
whatNotToDo: Do not call the number to 'cancel' the membership
Do not read out any one-time code to a person on the phone
Do not give remote access to your device to anyone claiming to be Amazon support

faqs.question: Does Amazon tell me about renewals by text with a link?
faqs.answer: Amazon membership and billing details normally appear inside your account, not in a text with a cancel link or phone number. An unexpected renewal text is a common scam pattern.

faqs.question: I am a Prime member, so could this be real?
faqs.answer: Scammers send these messages widely, so some reach real members by chance. Check your membership by signing in to Amazon directly rather than using the message.

faqs.question: Why do they want me to call a number?
faqs.answer: On the call they often pose as support and try to talk you through 'cancelling', which is used to collect your login, card, or one-time codes. Genuine cancellation is done in your account settings.

faqs.question: How do I report an Amazon Prime text scam?
faqs.answer: You can report it to Amazon through its official scam reporting page, forward it to your mobile provider's spam service, and notify your national anti-fraud centre.

title: Fake PayPal Email Scam

quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not click the link. Open PayPal yourself by typing the address or using the app to check your account.

Pressure to confirm your password, card or bank details to 'restore access'

Threats that your account will be closed within a short deadline
whatToDo: Do not click the link or enter your login details
Open PayPal directly by typing paypal.com or using the official app to check for any genuine notices
Forward the suspicious email to PayPal's reporting address and then delete it
Make sure two-step verification is switched on for your account
ifYouClicked: Do not enter any further details on the page
Change your PayPal password immediately, and anywhere you reused it
Turn on two-step verification and review linked cards and bank accounts
Watch your statements and report any unexpected transactions to PayPal and your bank
whatNotToDo: Do not reply to the email with any personal information
Do not call any phone number listed in the email
Do not enter verification codes on a page you reached through the link

faqs.question: Does PayPal limit accounts by email like this?
faqs.answer: PayPal does sometimes contact users about account issues, but a genuine notice can always be confirmed by logging in directly. An email pushing you to a link to 'confirm' your password is a common phishing pattern.

faqs.question: The email uses the PayPal logo, so is it genuine?
faqs.answer: Logos and branding are easy to copy. Scammers often reproduce the PayPal look exactly. Judge the message by where its links go and whether it asks for sensitive details, not by its appearance.

faqs.question: How can I tell a real PayPal email from a fake one?
faqs.answer: Real PayPal emails normally greet you by your full name and never ask for your password by email. When in doubt, ignore the email's links and check your account through the official site or app.

faqs.question: What if I already entered my password?
faqs.answer: Change your PayPal password straight away and on any other account where you used it, then turn on two-step verification and contact PayPal to secure your account.

title: Microsoft Account Email Scam

Spelling, spacing or sender-address details that look slightly off

Open your account by typing the official Microsoft address or using a saved bookmark
Check your recent sign-in activity in your real account security settings
Report the email as phishing in your mail app, then delete it
ifYouClicked: Do not enter any more information on the page
Change your Microsoft password now, and anywhere you reused it
Turn on two-step verification and review recent sign-in activity
Sign out of all sessions and update your account recovery details
whatNotToDo: Do not reply to the email or call any number it gives
Do not approve any sign-in prompts you did not start
Do not enter verification codes on a page reached through the link

faqs.question: Does Microsoft send unusual sign-in emails?
faqs.answer: Microsoft does send security alerts, but a genuine one can always be checked by signing in directly. A message demanding you act through its link to avoid closure is a common phishing approach.

faqs.question: The link looks like a Microsoft address, is it safe?
faqs.answer: Scammers use lookalike domains and hidden links that display real-looking text but lead elsewhere. Rather than trusting the link, reach your account through the official site or app.

faqs.question: Why would a scammer want my Microsoft login?
faqs.answer: A Microsoft or Outlook account often unlocks email, files and other linked services, and can be used to reset passwords elsewhere. That makes these logins a frequent target.

faqs.question: What if I entered my password already?
faqs.answer: Change it immediately, enable two-step verification, sign out of all sessions and review your recovery email and phone number for any unauthorised changes.

title: Fake DocuSign Email Scam

A prompt to log in with your email password to view the file
whatToDo: Do not click the link or sign in to view the document
If you expected something, contact the sender through a known, separate channel to confirm
Open DocuSign directly and use its access-code feature to find genuine documents
Report the email as phishing and then delete it
ifYouClicked: Do not enter any login details or download any attachment
If you entered a password, change it and anywhere you reused it
Run a security scan if a file downloaded to your device
Turn on two-step verification on your email and watch for unusual activity
whatNotToDo: Do not enable macros or 'editing' in any downloaded document
Do not reply with personal or company information
Do not forward the document to colleagues before confirming it is genuine

faqs.question: How do real DocuSign requests work?
faqs.answer: Genuine documents can be opened on the official DocuSign site using a unique access code, without entering your email password. An email asking for your password to view a file is a warning sign.

faqs.question: It looks like it came from a real company, is it safe?
faqs.answer: Scammers often spoof familiar names and copy DocuSign's layout. Treat an unexpected request cautiously and confirm with the supposed sender before opening anything.

faqs.question: Why is this scam used against businesses?
faqs.answer: Staff are used to signing documents, so a fake request can seem routine. Stolen logins can then be used to access email, payroll or company systems.

faqs.question: What if I clicked but did not sign in?
faqs.answer: Avoid entering any details, close the page and scan your device if anything downloaded. As a precaution, change your email password and switch on two-step verification.

title: Fake LinkedIn Email Scam

An unexpectedly attractive job offer or recruiter message you did not seek out
Pressure to sign in quickly to read a message or claim an opportunity

Generic wording and a sender address that does not match LinkedIn
whatToDo: Do not click the link or sign in through the email
Open LinkedIn directly via the app or website to see any genuine messages
Verify any recruiter by checking their profile and the company independently
Report the email as phishing and delete it
ifYouClicked: Do not enter any further information on the page
Change your LinkedIn password and anywhere you reused it
Turn on two-step verification and review active sessions and connected apps
Stay alert for follow-up scam messages using your stolen details
whatNotToDo: Do not move a 'job' conversation to private chat without verifying the recruiter

faqs.question: Does LinkedIn email me about messages and searches?
faqs.answer: LinkedIn does send notification emails, but you can always check the same information by opening the app or site directly. Treat the email as a prompt to log in yourself, not to click its links.

faqs.question: A recruiter contacted me with a great offer, is it real?
faqs.answer: It may be, but scammers pose as recruiters to harvest details or push fees. Verify the person and company independently, and be cautious if you are rushed or asked to pay anything.

faqs.question: Why target LinkedIn accounts?
faqs.answer: A LinkedIn login gives access to your professional network and can be used to send convincing scam messages to your contacts, or to support fake job and recruitment schemes.

faqs.question: What if I entered my login on the page?
faqs.answer: Change your LinkedIn password right away and anywhere you reused it, enable two-step verification, and review your active sessions for anything you do not recognise.

title: Social Media Shopping Ad Scam
metaTitle: Social Media Shopping Ad Scam: Red Flags & Tips
metaDescription: Learn how too-good-to-be-true social media shopping ads work, see an example pattern, and find out what to do if you ordered and received nothing or a counterfeit.
summary: This scam uses eye-catching, heavily discounted product ads in social media feeds to lure you to fake or dishonest online stores that take your payment and deliver nothing, or send a cheap counterfeit instead.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: A social media ad offering a popular product at an unrealistically low price from a store you have never heard of.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not rush to buy. Research the store's name and reviews independently before entering any payment details.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'FLASH SALE - 80% OFF today only! Premium [product] going fast, almost sold out. Order now before stock runs out: [unfamiliar link]'
redFlags: Discounts that seem far too large for a popular or branded product
A store name you cannot find any independent reviews or history for
Heavy countdown timers and 'almost sold out' pressure in the ad
No clear contact address, returns policy or company details on the site
Payment only by methods that are hard to dispute, such as bank transfer
whatToDo: Search the store's name alongside words like 'review' or 'scam' before buying
Check for a genuine address, returns policy and working contact details
Pay using a method with buyer protection, such as a credit card, where possible
Take screenshots of the ad, listing and order in case you need to dispute it
ifYouClicked: Avoid entering card details if the site shows several warning signs
If you paid, contact your bank or card provider about a possible chargeback
Save all order confirmations, adverts and messages as evidence
Report the ad to the social media platform and your national consumer body
whatNotToDo: Do not pay by bank transfer or gift card to an unknown store
Do not reuse a password you use elsewhere when creating an account
Do not ignore a much-too-cheap price just because the ad looks professional

faqs.question: Are all heavily discounted social media ads scams?
faqs.answer: No, but very large discounts on popular items from unknown stores are a common warning sign. It is worth checking the seller independently before buying rather than trusting the ad alone.

faqs.question: The ad has lots of likes and good comments, is it trustworthy?
faqs.answer: Engagement and reviews can be faked or bought. Look for independent reviews away from the ad, and be cautious if the only positive feedback appears on the seller's own pages.

faqs.question: I received a counterfeit instead of the real item, what now?
faqs.answer: Keep all evidence and contact your bank or card provider about a chargeback. You can also report the seller to the platform and to your national consumer protection body.

faqs.question: How can I shop more safely from social media ads?
faqs.answer: Research the store first, prefer payment methods with buyer protection, check the returns policy, and be wary of urgency and prices that look too good to be true.

title: Zelle Payment Scam
metaTitle: Zelle Payment Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
metaDescription: Learn how Zelle payment scams use fake bank fraud alerts to trick you into sending money, the red flags to watch for, and what to do if you sent a payment.
summary: In this scam someone posing as your bank's fraud team contacts you about 'suspicious activity' and pressures you to send money through Zelle to 'reverse' a charge or 'protect' your account. Zelle transfers are usually instant and hard to recover.

quickVerdict.mainRedFlag: Someone claiming to be your bank tells you to send a Zelle payment to 'cancel', 'reverse', or 'protect' your money.
quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Hang up or stop replying, then call your bank using the number on the back of your card to check whether anything is wrong.

exampleMessage: Example pattern: 'BANK FRAUD ALERT: We blocked a $480 charge. To reverse it, send a Zelle payment to your own number now or the charge will go through. Reply STOP to decline.'
redFlags: A caller or text says you must send a Zelle payment to 'cancel' or 'reverse' fraud
Pressure to act within minutes before a charge 'goes through'
A request to send money 'to yourself' or to a phone number or email you do not recognise
The contact comes to you unexpectedly rather than you contacting the bank
You are asked to read out a code, PIN, or one-time passcode to complete the 'reversal'
whatToDo: Stop the conversation and do not send any payment
Call your bank directly using the number on your card or statement, not a number the caller gave you
Ask the bank to confirm whether there is any real issue on your account
Report the attempt to your bank and to your national anti-fraud centre
ifYouClicked: If you already sent a Zelle payment, contact your bank immediately and ask them to attempt a recall
Change your online banking password and any reused passwords
Tell your bank if you shared a one-time code or PIN so they can secure your account
Watch your account closely for further transfers and set up transaction alerts
whatNotToDo: Do not send money to 'reverse' or 'protect' a charge
Do not share one-time passcodes, PINs, or your full password
Do not trust caller ID, which can be faked to show your bank's name

faqs.question: Would my bank ever ask me to send myself a Zelle payment?
faqs.answer: Banks do not ask you to send money to yourself or anyone else to stop fraud. A request like this through a call or text is a common scam pattern.

faqs.question: Can a Zelle payment be reversed?
faqs.answer: Zelle transfers are usually instant and often cannot be reversed once sent. That is exactly why scammers favour it, so always confirm before sending.

faqs.question: The caller knew my name and bank. Does that make it real?
faqs.answer: Scammers can buy or guess personal details and fake caller ID to seem genuine. Knowing your details is not proof, so verify through official channels.

faqs.question: What should I do if I think I sent money to a scammer?
faqs.answer: Contact your bank right away to report it and ask whether the transfer can be recalled. The sooner you act, the better your chances.

title: Cash App Scam

quickVerdict.whatToDoFirst: Do not share any codes or send any money, and reach Cash App only through the app's own help section.

Being told to download a remote-access or screen-sharing app to 'fix' your account
Pressure to act fast before an offer or refund 'expires'
whatToDo: Ignore requests for your PIN, sign-in code, or upfront payments
Use only the in-app help in Cash App to contact real support
If you received an unexpected payment, do not refund it manually; let the sender request it through the app
Report and block the account, and report the scam to your national anti-fraud centre
ifYouClicked: If you shared your sign-in code or PIN, change your Cash App PIN and account password straight away
Remove any remote-access app you were told to install
Review recent activity and report any payments you did not make
Contact your linked bank or card provider if money left your account
whatNotToDo: Do not pay a fee to claim a prize or 'release' funds
Do not share your PIN or one-time sign-in code with anyone
Do not refund 'accidental' payments yourself or install apps a stranger suggests

faqs.question: Does Cash App run giveaways that need a payment first?
faqs.answer: Genuine promotions do not ask you to send money to receive a larger amount. A request to pay first is a common scam sign.

faqs.question: How can I tell real Cash App support from a fake?
faqs.answer: Real support is reached through the app's own help section. Cash App will not call or message you to ask for your PIN or sign-in code.

faqs.question: Someone sent me money by mistake and wants it back. Is that a scam?
faqs.answer: It can be. The 'payment' may later be reversed, leaving you out of pocket if you refunded it manually. Ask them to cancel it through the app instead.

faqs.question: What if I already gave away my code or PIN?
faqs.answer: Change your PIN and password immediately, review your activity, and report anything unfamiliar. Contact your linked bank if funds were taken.

title: Overpayment Scam
metaTitle: Overpayment Scam: Red Flags and What to Do
